subject: Polity
sub_topic: Major constitutional amendments and their impact

concepts.name: Article 368: Scope, Procedure, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Three-tier amendment procedure: simple majority, special majority, and special majority + state ratification
What Article 368 does NOT cover: provisions amendable by simple majority outside Article 368 (e.g., Articles 2, 3, 100, 169)
Distinction between 'constituent power' vs 'legislative power' as clarified in Sankari Prasad and Kesavananda Bharati
UPSC trap: State ratification requires only 50% of states (not all), and there is no time limit for ratification

concepts.name: 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951: Ninth Schedule and Reasonable Restrictions
key_dimensions: Addition of the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from judicial review under Fundamental Rights
Insertion of 'reasonable restrictions' clauses in Articles 19(2) and 19(4) — expanded grounds for restricting free speech
First instance of Parliament overriding a Supreme Court judgment (State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan)
Significance as the genesis of the Parliament vs. Judiciary conflict over constitutional supremacy

concepts.name: 7th Amendment Act, 1956: Reorganization of States and Its Constitutional Impact
key_dimensions: Abolished the four-tier classification of states (Parts A, B, C, D) and introduced States and Union Territories
Modified the concept of 'equal representation' in the Rajya Sabha — Schedule 4 revised
Enabled creation of common High Courts for two or more states (Article 231)
UPSC trap: This amendment required state ratification under Article 368 because it altered the Rajya Sabha representation

concepts.name: 24th Amendment Act, 1971: Parliament's Absolute Power to Amend Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Overruled Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) by amending Articles 13 and 368
Added clause to Article 13 explicitly stating that Article 368 amendments are NOT 'law' under Article 13
Made Presidential assent to constitutional amendment bills mandatory (removed discretion)
Partially upheld but subjected to Basic Structure doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

concepts.name: Basic Structure Doctrine: Origin, Evolution, and Unanswered Questions
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-judge bench, 7:6 majority establishing Basic Structure
Elements identified as Basic Structure: supremacy of Constitution, republican & democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, unity & integrity of India
UPSC trap: The Constitution does NOT explicitly mention Basic Structure — it is entirely judge-made law
Ongoing controversy: No exhaustive/codified list of Basic Structure elements; each case adds new elements (e.g., free and fair elections in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975)

concepts.name: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: The 'Mini Constitution' and Its Sweeping Changes
key_dimensions: Added 'Socialist,' 'Secular,' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble
Added Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) — 10 duties originally
Gave Parliament absolute power to amend any part of Constitution including Basic Structure (Clauses 4 & 5 of Article 368) — later struck down in Minerva Mills
Expanded the Ninth Schedule, curtailed High Court powers of judicial review, extended Lok Sabha and state assembly terms to 6 years, and introduced Articles 31C (expanded)

concepts.name: 44th Amendment Act, 1978: Restoration of Democratic Safeguards Post-Emergency
key_dimensions: Deleted Right to Property from Fundamental Rights (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) — made a legal right under Article 300A
Restored original 5-year term for Lok Sabha and state assemblies
Strengthened provisions against misuse of Emergency: President must act on Cabinet's written advice; Lok Sabha can revoke Emergency by simple majority
UPSC trap: Article 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during Emergency — added by this amendment

concepts.name: 52nd Amendment Act, 1985: Anti-Defection Law and the Tenth Schedule
key_dimensions: Added Tenth Schedule providing for disqualification of members on grounds of defection
Original provisions: merger required 1/3rd of party members (later changed to 2/3rd by 91st Amendment)
Speaker/Chairman as the adjudicating authority — constitutionality challenged (Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu, 1992: upheld but Speaker's order subject to judicial review)
UPSC trap: The Tenth Schedule was added by a constitutional amendment but does NOT require state ratification despite affecting federalism

concepts.name: 61st Amendment Act, 1988: Lowering Voting Age from 21 to 18
key_dimensions: Amended Article 326 to lower voting age for Lok Sabha and state assembly elections
Aimed at enfranchising youth bulge; India adopted universal adult franchise at a lower age than many democracies
UPSC trap: This required only special majority under Article 368 — does NOT fall under the state ratification category despite affecting elections
Comparison angle: Voting age ≠ age of candidacy (still 25 for Lok Sabha/Assembly, 30 for Rajya Sabha/Council)

concepts.name: 73rd and 74th Amendment Acts, 1992: Constitutionalization of Local Self-Government
key_dimensions: Added Parts IX and IX-A; Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects for Panchayats) and Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects for Municipalities)
Mandatory provisions vs. voluntary provisions — States MUST implement reservation, direct elections, and State Election Commission; but devolution of functions is discretionary
UPSC trap: These amendments required state ratification under Article 368 because they affected state legislative lists
Creation of State Finance Commission and District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) — often confused with State Planning Commission

concepts.name: 86th Amendment Act, 2002: Right to Education and Its Three-Dimensional Impact
key_dimensions: Inserted Article 21A: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years as a Fundamental Right
Amended Article 45: Changed directive from early childhood care (0–6) to focus on children below 6
Amended Article 51A: Added duty of parents/guardians to provide education opportunities to children (Fundamental Duty)
UPSC trap: Children below 6 years are EXCLUDED from Article 21A; their care remains a DPSP under Article 45

concepts.name: 91st Amendment Act, 2003: Anti-Defection Law Reforms and Cabinet Size Cap
key_dimensions: Changed merger threshold from 1/3rd to 2/3rd of party members to prevent political horse-trading
Inserted Article 75(1A): Cabinet size capped at 15% of total Lok Sabha strength (minimum 12 for states)
Abolished provision for exemption from disqualification on the ground of split
UPSC trap: The 15% cap applies separately to the Union Council of Ministers and each State Council of Ministers

concepts.name: 99th Amendment Act, 2014 and the NJAC Judgment (2015): Judicial Appointments Controversy
key_dimensions: Replaced Collegium system with National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) — 6-member body including Law Minister and two eminent persons
Supreme Court struck it down in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) as violating judicial independence (Basic Structure)
Core conflict: Executive vs. Judiciary in judicial appointments; 'primacy of judiciary' declared a Basic Structure element
UPSC trap: The 99th Amendment had been ratified by more than half the states yet was struck down — demonstrating that correct procedure does NOT protect against Basic Structure violations

concepts.name: 100th Amendment Act, 2015: Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh
key_dimensions: Gave effect to Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) of 1974 between India and Bangladesh — exchange of enclaves
India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh; Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India
Required amendment to First Schedule (territorial description of states) — affected Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura
UPSC trap: Since it amended the First Schedule affecting state territories, it required state ratification — the four affected states ratified it

concepts.name: 101st Amendment Act, 2016: Goods and Services Tax and Fiscal Federalism
key_dimensions: Inserted Articles 246A, 269A, 279A; amended Articles 248, 268, 269, 270, 271, 286, 366, 368, and Sixth/Seventh Schedules
Created concurrent taxing powers for Centre and States on supply of goods and services (Article 246A) — unprecedented in Indian federalism
GST Council (Article 279A): Voting weightage — Centre has 1/3rd, States collectively have 2/3rd; decisions by 3/4th majority
UPSC trap: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption and petroleum products are EXCLUDED from GST; five petroleum products included later through GST Council recommendation

concepts.name: 102nd and 105th Amendment Acts: OBC Commission and Reservation in Promotions
key_dimensions: 102nd Amendment (2018): Gave constitutional status to National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B) and defined 'socially and educationally backward classes' in Article 342A
105th Amendment (2021): Restored states' power to identify SEBCs for their own lists — reversed Supreme Court's Maratha reservation judgment (Maharashtra v. Indra Sawhney II)

UPSC trap: 102nd Amendment created ambiguity — SC in Jahnavi Sekhri case (2021) held that ONLY the President (Central list) can notify OBCs, removing state power; 105th Amendment was enacted specifically to reverse this
Distinction: NCBC under 102nd Amendment ≠ NCBC under the earlier statutory act of 1993

concepts.name: Ninth Schedule: Judicial Review Immunity and the I.R. Coelho Judgment
key_dimensions: Originally designed to protect land reform laws; gradually expanded to protect laws from diverse subjects (banking, industrial relations, reservations)

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): 9-judge bench ruled that laws added to Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati date) are subject to judicial review if they violate Basic Structure
UPSC trap: Laws added BEFORE April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute protection; those added AFTER can be challenged
Political misuse angle: Ninth Schedule grew from 13 laws (1951) to 284 laws — used to shield even non-agrarian laws from judicial scrutiny

concepts.name: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Limits on Parliament's Amending Power
key_dimensions: Struck down Clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368 inserted by 42nd Amendment — Parliament cannot confer on itself unlimited amending power
Struck down expanded Article 31C (which gave DPSPs primacy over ALL Fundamental Rights) — restored balance between Parts III and IV
Established 'harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs' as a Basic Structure element
UPSC trap: Original Article 31C (from 25th Amendment, protecting Articles 39(b) and 39(c)) was upheld; only the EXPANDED version was struck down

concepts.name: 104th Amendment Act, 2019: Extension of Reservation for SC/ST and Abolition of Anglo-Indian Nomination
key_dimensions: Extended reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and state assemblies for another 10 years (from 2020 to 2030) — amended Article 334
Abolished the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha (Article 331) and state assemblies (Article 333)
UPSC trap: The 104th Amendment removed Anglo-Indian representation but reservation for SCs/STs was EXTENDED, not removed — common confusion point
Broader context: Anglo-Indian nominated seats were continued through successive amendments since 1950; the community's population had significantly declined

concepts.name: Doctrine of Implied Limitations and the Golak Nath–Kesavananda–Minerva Mills Trilogy
key_dimensions: Golak Nath (1967): Fundamental Rights cannot be amended at all — Parliament has no constituent power over FR; prospective overruling applied
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament CAN amend any part including FR but CANNOT destroy Basic Structure — 'amend' means improve, not destroy
Minerva Mills (1980): Reinforced Basic Structure; added that limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure element — creating a self-referential protection
UPSC trap: The sequence matters — each judgment both responded to and was anticipated by a constitutional amendment (Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills)
